analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending and gives public vouchers to candidates who accept limits on PAC and big-donor money.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to five House committees and two subcommittees in March 1996 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill set up a voluntary system for House campaigns: candidates who agreed to a $600,000 spending cap and tight limits on PAC and large-donor money would receive publicly funded 'voter communication vouchers' of up to $200,000, matched to small-dollar contributions. It also banned national party 'soft money,' restricted fundraising by federal officeholders, tightened disclosure rules, required timely reporting of last-minute independent attacks, and made lobbying organizations disclose the contributions they collect. It was referred to five House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and died without any hearing result or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in House races, and candidates who rely on small donations rather than PACs, big donors, or party soft money. Candidates facing independent attack ads would get extra voucher money to respond, and every candidate receiving vouchers would have to closed-caption their TV ads and take part in at least two debates.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who limit their own contributions to $25,000 and stay under a $600,000 spending cap would receive voter communication vouchers of up to $200,000, matched to small individual contributions of up to $250 each, so campaigns would not depend on large donors. [S2, S3]

The bill bans national party committees from raising or spending soft money — the unlimited, unregulated contributions that flooded federal elections — and restricts fundraising by federal candidates and officeholders for soft-money organizations. [S2, S3]

A House candidate hit by independent expenditures of $10,000 or more would get additional vouchers to answer them, and broadcasters would have to hand attack-ad scripts to the targeted candidate within days and offer a chance to respond. [S2, S3]

Organizations that lobby Congress would have to disclose the contributions they receive, bundling of contributions would be restricted, cash contributions over $100 would be prohibited, and the FEC could go to court for injunctions against violations in progress. [S2, S3]

analysis.who_pays: PACs, large individual donors, and national party committees that relied on unlimited soft money would lose a large channel of influence. Broadcasters and cable operators would face new duties to disclose attack ads and offer response time. The voucher fund would be financed through a voluntary tax-filing checkoff, inflation-adjusted federal civil penalties, and small royalties on affinity credit cards.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, big donors, party committees, broadcasters

drawbacks.text: The system is voluntary: a wealthy or heavily funded candidate who declines to participate faces no limits at all, and the bill only partially responds to this — if an opponent spends over 25 percent of the cap, the participating candidate's limits are lifted, effectively returning the race to an arms race rather than reducing total spending. [S3]

Mandatory spending limits on campaign speech raise First Amendment concerns; the bill itself anticipated this by providing expedited Supreme Court review of constitutional questions, acknowledging that parts of the scheme could be struck down. [S2, S3]

The FEC would audit only about 5 percent of eligible candidates after each election, and enforcement relies on civil penalties rather than criminal sanctions, which critics of campaign-finance laws argue invites violations by campaigns that can afford the fines. [S3]

The $200,000 voucher maximum is small relative to the cost of media markets in many districts, so candidates in expensive markets would still be pressed to raise money beyond small contributions. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the main channels through which organized money reaches House campaigns — soft money, PACs, bundling, and shadowy independent spending — and gives candidates a public funding route to run competitive races. Its real weakness is that participation is voluntary, so a race involving a self-funded or non-participating candidate reverts to no limits at all, and enforcement depends on a small audit program and civil fines. Still, as a designed system, it would have made House campaigns more dependent on voters and less dependent on concentrated donors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees and forwarded to two subcommittees in March 1996, and neither the full committees nor the House ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey (D-MA) introduced the bill on March 7, 1996, and it was referred to the House Oversight Committee and, in addition, to the Commerce, Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Government Reform and Oversight committees. [S1, S5]
On March 18, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance and the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology, where it remained. [S5]
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a House Democrat, in addition to its sponsor. [S4]
No further action was recorded, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, without a vote in either chamber. [S1, S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, large donors, and national party committees that rely on soft money kept the existing rules and their influence intact; the House members whose campaigns benefit from those channels were spared a vote on the limits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs, big donors, and soft-money party committees

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Citizen Representative Act of 1996 and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Oversight Committee and four additional committees (Commerce, Judiciary, Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 7, 1996, and took no further action beyond referrals.

against.name: Subcommittees on Telecommunications and Finance and on Government Management, Information and Technology
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 18, 1996, and reported no hearings, markup, or action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and it was never brought up in committee or on the House floor.

industries.industry: Political action committees and large individual donors
industries.note: The bill would cap PAC contributions at $90,000 per election cycle and large-donor contributions at $120,000, and restrict bundling and cash over $100 — cutting off the largest channels of organized money into House races. Their influence over candidates would shrink in direct proportion to voters' relative weight. [S2, S3]

The bill bans national parties from soliciting or spending soft money and forces all spending that could affect federal elections into regulated, reported funds. Parties would lose the ability to accept unlimited checks from wealthy donors and corporations. [S2, S3]

Groups that lobby Congress would have to disclose the contributions they receive as political committees do, and lobbyists could no longer count as independent spenders or fundraising conduits. Their ability to move money into elections anonymously would narrow. [S2, S3]

They would face new duties to hand scripts of attack ads against voucher candidates to those candidates within days and to sell response time at standard rates, plus revised candidate-rate and preemption rules. The costs are modest but the obligations cut against editorial and commercial discretion. [S2, S3]

Spending caps, bundling restrictions, limits on personal services pass-through reporting, and audit requirements would shrink the total pool of campaign money consultants and professional fundraisers are paid from. [S2, S3]
